A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OmniResponse model and ResponseNet dataset. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reordering.

before.justification: v1 reports original ResponseNet benchmark results, component ablations in Table 3, and generated conversational examples in Figure 5.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds human preference results, runtime measurements, demographic analysis, and additional synchronization scores.

M1.justification: The Phi-3.5-based architecture, Chrono-Text Markup, TempoVoice, causal attention, training losses, and generation procedure are retained. Rewording the methodological appendix does not introduce a different component or procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 696-interaction ResponseNet corpus for online multimodal conversational response generation. Added demographics describe existing data; the human ratings and runtime measurements do not establish a new conversational domain, dataset, or input scenario.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Qwen-7B-Chat, Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and DeepSeek-R1 to the retained comparators. The new runtime comparison in Table 6 additionally includes SadTalker and a row named Hallo, whose reference identifies Hallo3. This substantially broadens the comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 49-participant A/B study with 16 randomly ordered clips per participant and four assessment criteria, an inference benchmark on one A100 80GB, and LSE-C evaluation. The original 417/139/140 data splits and 2,000-epoch training schedule remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a demographic-composition analysis covering identities, gender, ethnicity, and age bands. The Chrono-Text/TempoVoice ablations and Figure 5 qualitative case remain unchanged; no demographic performance or fairness test accompanies the new composition analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new preference percentages and demographic counts are descriptive results, while LSE-C measures synchronization confidence rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: All retained Table 2 model scores and Table 3 ablation values are unchanged. Substantial new results include four text-baseline rows, human preferences of 67.3–95.9%, OmniResponse throughput of 15.62 FPS, and LSE-C scores of 0.371 versus 0.157 for LSTM and 0.269 for Audio-Visual LLM. Table 8 also reports demographic results for 161 identities.

T1.justification: The problem formulation and mathematical expressions, including Equations 1–6, are retained. Clarifying the description of the sampling factor and adjusting notation do not introduce new mathematical reasoning, assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain an online model producing synchronized verbal and nonverbal responses through Chrono-Text and TempoVoice, plus the ResponseNet benchmark. Abstract and conclusion edits preserve the scientific scope and novelty claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.1 newly attributes improved nonverbal realism to using text as an intermediate modality. Appendix E.1 explains that appropriate listener silence depresses LSE-C, limiting its suitability as a primary metric. The existing limitations are retained and moved into Section 6.

D1.justification: v2 newly states that code, models, and data are publicly available, identifies snapshots for some added comparators, and documents inference hardware, omitted deployment optimizations, and use of the official SyncNet script. LoRA rank 64 and alpha 16 were already disclosed in v1 Appendix A.

R1.justification: References expand to cover the new comparators, ReactDiff, REACT2025, MakeItTalk, and misuse protections; Kington et al. and Meta-Transformer are removed. The basic positioning against single-modality generation remains, with limited updates rather than a new research framing.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and Appendix B.3, condenses related work, and corrects wording and cross-references. It moves limitations and risks into the conclusion and places references after the appendices. Most of the narrative and methodological exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds compact tables for preferences, runtime, demographics, and SyncNet scores, expands Table 2, and enlarges and relocates Table 3. Figures 1–9 retain their content with resizing and placement adjustments; the overall visual design remains stable.

improvement.justification: The human study and runtime measurements add perceptual and practical evidence absent from v1, while demographic reporting and the SyncNet discussion improve transparency. Their evidential strength remains limited by missing uncertainty reporting and differing generation settings in the runtime comparison. Section 5.4 also misidentifies the 67.3% preference as speech appropriateness, whereas Table 4 assigns it to visual quality. These issues temper a positive overall gain.
